newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU ministers meet amid Albania crisis.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers meet amid Albania crisis.

text.p: The crisis in Albania looked set to capture the agenda on Saturday at an informal meeting of European Union foreign ministers in the central Dutch countryside.
Ministers from across the 15-nation bloc, gathering for what is supposed to be a relaxed chat about foreign policy, were expected to discuss the situation and Tirana's call for help from the West.
OSCE mediator Franz Vranitzky said on Friday that there was no alternative to foreign intervention to halt Albania's descent into chaos.
Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, hosting the Apeldoorn meeting, said the EU was not ruling anything out and that his colleagues would be considering a number of options.
But EU officials said there was no sign that any country in the bloc had the appetite to become involved militarily.
"Does the West want to go into Albania? Who are we going to help?" one EU diplomat said ahead of the meeting.

Officials said the EU ministers were likely to throw their support behind the mediation efforts of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), whose current president, Denmark, is an EU member.
"The common aspect of what has been said in the EU, NATO and at the United Nations is that the OSCE should have the lead role," the diplomat said.
There were also growing signs among some in the EU that Albania would be best served if President Sali Berisha quit.

Despite the evident need for ministers to discuss Albania, officials said van Mierlo was hoping the issue would not hijack the two-day meeting at which he wanted to focus on some long-term EU dilemmas.
The ministers were expected to discuss EU plans for bringing in countries from the former communist bloc and the relationship with NATO enlargement plans.

Although no formal decisions were to be taken, the ministers were expected to discuss whether enlargement talks should begin with 10 former communist applicants at once, or whether the bloc should differentiate between those countries who were clearly ready and those who were not.
Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Slovenia, Lithuania, Estonia, Bulgaria, Romania and Latvia have all been promised eventual EU membership.

The concern in some EU capitals is that the EU and NATO should not find themselves in a position where they have effectively rejected any of the countries by focusing on the favourites for membership -- Warsaw, Prague and Budapest.
On Sunday, the ministers were due to turn their attention to relations with Turkey, recently snubbed by Christian Democrat leaders from the EU.
